## Three notes can run a whole melody

Take a three-note cell and repeat it two semitones higher. You'll spot the
connection instantly. Double its durations and recognition slows down without
disappearing. Keep only the first two notes and the fragment still points back
at where it came from. One small object, several different disguises, and your
ear tracks it through all of them.

A *motive* is a short musical idea that survives transformation. A *sequence*
restates it at a new pitch level. *Development* is what happens when you apply
operations like transposition, inversion, augmentation and fragmentation until
repeated material starts having consequences. The first plain statement tells
you what the object is. Everything after that tells you how far its identity
bends before it breaks.

## Eight bars from one cell

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 108
use_synth :pluck

cell = [60, 63, 62]
rhythm = [0.5, 0.5, 1]

define :play_phrase do |notes, durations|
  notes.zip(durations).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
end

define :transpose_notes do |notes, amount|
  notes.map { |pitch| pitch + amount }
end

define :invert_notes do |notes, axis|
  notes.map { |pitch| axis - (pitch - axis) }
end

bars = [
  [cell, rhythm],
  [transpose_notes(cell, 2), rhythm],
  [transpose_notes(cell, 5), rhythm],
  [invert_notes(cell, cell[0]), rhythm],
  [cell, rhythm.map { |duration| duration * 2 }],
  [cell.first(2) * 2, [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]],
  [transpose_notes(invert_notes(cell, cell[0]), 7), rhythm],
  [[60, 63, 62, 60], [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5]]
]

2.times do
  bars.each { |notes, durations| play_phrase notes, durations }
end
```

The cell comes back at new pitch levels, reflected around an axis, stretched to
twice its length, and cut down to a fragment. Repeat the eight-bar plan once and
a single source object has supplied you with sixteen bars of melody. Recognition
arrives at different speeds along the way: transposition announces itself almost
immediately, while inversion and fragmentation sometimes land only after the
cell has already finished. Which bar is the first one where you lose the thread?

## Crowd it, reflect it, wear it out

1. Change the sequence offsets from `2` and `5` to `1` and `2`. The entries now
   crowd together. Listen for whether they still read as statements at distinct
   levels or merge into one long rising thought.

2. Move the inversion axis from the first note to 63. Reflection follows the
   same signed-distance rule and lands somewhere else entirely, which shows you
   that an operation and its reference point are two separate decisions.

3. Repeat the unaltered cell four times in a row. Mark the exact bar where
   repetition stops confirming the idea and starts holding the music still. Then
   play the developed version again and compare that span.

## What each operation keeps

Transposition adds a constant to every pitch and preserves all the intervals.
Inversion reflects signed distances around an axis, so an upward minor third
becomes a downward one. Augmentation scales duration. Fragmentation selects a
subsequence. Each operation keeps some invariants and releases others, which is
exactly why the motive can stay present without ever returning unchanged.

The `bars` array holds your compositional decisions and `play_phrase` handles
realisation. Every transformed passage derives from `cell` and none of them are
copied literals, so editing the source changes all its descendants at once. Try
it: change `cell` to `[60, 64, 62]` and the whole sixteen bars reorganise around
a major third. Repairing scattered copies by hand would have cost you the
experiment.

A sequence becomes legible through recurrence at successive pitch levels. Two
statements usually establish the rule, further ones confirm it, and enough of
them exhaust it. There's no universal count for where that tips over. Because
both the offsets and the repeat count are editable, you can audition the
judgement in this phrase instead of inheriting it as advice.

Placement changes what a transformation means. A transposed cell sitting next to
its source behaves like continuation. The identical data several bars later
feels like recollection. Register, cadence and accompaniment all strengthen or
weaken that relation. Your transformation functions capture local pitch and
duration rules; the `bars` plan gives each result a position in time, and
position is half of what the listener responds to.

The closing bar extends the cell by appending C to the end. Put the same extra
note at the front and the original three notes stop sounding like a beginning,
even though every value is still there. Recognition depends on boundaries and
emphasis as much as on membership, so development is partly a question of where
you let the preserved material speak.

## Sixteen bars, one source array

Build a sixteen-bar plan out of a single four-note motive. Include a literal
return, a three-stage sequence, one inversion, one augmented statement and a
two-note fragment. Derive every altered pitch list through your functions and
copy no resulting values into the plan.

Print a label before each bar, then run it once without watching the log and
note which transformations announced themselves and which slipped past. Compare
that list against the labels afterwards. Where the two disagree, you've found
the point where a transformation you can see in the source stopped being a
transformation you can hear.
